'''Margaret-Ann Armour''' {{postnominals|CM}} (6 September 1939 – 25 May 2019) was a [[Scotland|Scottish]]-born [[Canadian]] chemist based at the [[University of Alberta]]. She is best known for her expertise in developing guidelines for hazardous lab waste disposal, and for being a vocal advocate for women in science. Armour founded the Women in Scholarship, Engineering, Science and Technology (WISEST) program, and served as the first and only Associate Dean of Science for Diversity at the University of Alberta. Among her many honors, she was named a member of the [[Order of Canada]] (2006), a [[3M Teaching Fellow]] (1996) and a Canada 150 ambassador (2017).

==Early life and education==
Armour was born in [[Glasgow]], Scotland on 6 September 1939,<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://www.folio.ca/university-mourns-loss-of-passionate-promoter-of-women-in-science-and-tech/|title=University mourns loss of passionate promoter of women in science and tech|website=University mourns loss of passionate promoter of women in science and tech|access-date=2019-05-26}}</ref><ref name=":8" /> Her father died during [[World War II]], and she was raised by her mother (a teacher).<ref name=":8" /> Armour and her mother lived in a town between [[Dundee]] and [[Aberdeen]], before moving to [[Penicuik]], where Armour attended the nearby [[Lasswade High School Centre|Lasswade Secondary School]].<ref name=":8" /> Her natural curiosity for science was fostered there by her chemistry teacher Pop Davidson.<ref name=":8" /> Armour went on to pursue a [[Bachelor of Science]] at the [[University of Edinburgh]], then spent five years working as research chemist in the paper-making industry at Penicuik, where her research into finding different paper coatings resulted in Armour being awarded a [[Master of Science]] from the University of Edinburgh.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":8" /><ref name=":5" />

In 1970, Armour completed her PhD in organic chemistry at the [[University of Alberta]] in [[Canada]].<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":8" /><ref name=":5">{{Cite web|url=https://www.ualberta.ca/chemistry/news-and-events/lecture-series/margaret-ann-armour-lecture-series|title=Margaret-Ann Armour Lecture Series {{!}} Faculty of Science|website=www.ualberta.ca|access-date=2019-05-26|archive-date=2019-05-26|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190526075943/https://www.ualberta.ca/chemistry/news-and-events/lecture-series/margaret-ann-armour-lecture-series|url-status=dead}}</ref> She completed a post-doctoral fellowship at the University of Edinburgh, under the supervision of [[John Cadogan]].<ref name=":8" />

==Career==
In 1979, Armour joined the University of Alberta's Department of Chemistry, where she was one of the few female professors in the university's Faculty of Science.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":5" /><ref name=":2">{{Cite web|url=https://www.ualberta.ca/canada-150/bio-margaret-ann-armour|title=Margaret-Ann Armour: the champion {{!}} University of Alberta|website=www.ualberta.ca|access-date=2019-05-26}}</ref><ref name=":6">{{Cite web|url=http://www.financialpost.com/executive/women/wxn/detail.html?id=129|title=WXN Award Winners {{!}} Women Executives {{!}} Executive {{!}} Financial Post|website=www.financialpost.com|access-date=2019-05-26|archive-date=2019-05-28|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190528051401/http://www.financialpost.com/executive/women/wxn/detail.html?id=129|url-status=dead}}</ref> Armour supervised undergraduate organic chemistry laboratory courses.<ref name=":8" /><ref name=":6" /> Her research explored how to dispose of dangerous waste, where she published several guidelines including the Hazardous Laboratory Chemicals Disposal Guide.<ref name=":8" />

In 1982, Armour was leading a committee to explore how to increase the number of women in science, which led her to found the Women in Scholarship, Engineering, Science and Technology (WISEST) program.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":8">{{Cite web|url=https://www.astech.ca/archives/indexofpastwinners/armour-dr-margaret-ann|title=Armour, Dr. Margaret-Ann – ASTech Foundation|access-date=2019-05-26}}</ref><ref name=":2" /> WISEST initiatives seek to promote diversity in the STEM fields through engagement, education and application.<ref name=":8" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ualberta.ca/services/wisest|title=Women in Scholarship, Engineering, Science, and Technology {{!}} University of Alberta|website=www.ualberta.ca|access-date=2019-05-26}}</ref> WISEST's efforts have been recognized by various awards, including a Michael Smith Award for Science Promotion (1994), the [[Royal Society of Canada]]'s McNeil Medal, and Alberta Science and Technology Awards Foundation's Excellence in Science and Technology Public Awareness Prize (1996).<ref name=":5" /><ref name=":6" /><ref name=":3">{{Cite web|url=https://3mcouncil.stlhe.ca/resources/3m-fellows/award-winners/1996armour/|title=Margaret-Ann Armour (1996) {{!}} 3M National Teaching and Learning Fellows|access-date=2019-05-26}}</ref>

Armour served as the assistant chair of the Department of Chemistry (1989–2005) before assuming the role of the University of Alberta's Associate Dean of Science for Diversity in 2005.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":6" /><ref name=":10">{{Cite web|url=https://www.ualberta.ca/science/about-us/contours/2016-fall-contours/2016/october/faculty-of-science-diversity-report|title=Faculty of Science Diversity Report {{!}} Faculty of Science|website=www.ualberta.ca|access-date=2019-05-26}}</ref> Armour is the first and only person to serve as the Associate Dean of Science for Diversity in the university.<ref name=":2" /> In this position, Armour developed 13 initiatives, including Project Catalyst, which is a program to increase the representation of women in faculty positions within the University of Alberta's Faculty of Science.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":5" /><ref name=":10" /> Since 2005, Armour oversaw the recruitment of 14 women (out of 37 faculty positions in total).<ref name=":10" />

On April 6, 2006, Armour was named a member of the [[Order of Canada]].<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":4">{{Cite web|url=https://www.gg.ca/en/honours/recipients/146-8852|title=Ms. Margaret-Ann Armour, C.M.|website=The Governor General of Canada|access-date=2019-05-26}}</ref> Among her many awards, she has notably been recognized as a [[3M]] Teaching Fellow (1996), one of the 100 Edmontonians of the Century and a Canada 150 ambassador by the Government of Canada in 2017.<ref name=":5" /><ref name=":2" /><ref name=":6" /><ref name=":3" /><ref name=":9">{{Cite web|url=https://concordia.ab.ca/about/who-we-are/leadership/board-of-governors/honorary-degrees/recipients/margaret-ann-armour/|title=Convocation 2019|website=Concordia University of Edmonton|access-date=2019-05-26}}</ref> Armour has previously been recognized in [[Maclean's]] ''Ten Canadians Making a Difference'' list (2003), in the ''Who's Who of Canadian Women 1999–2000'' book, and twice in Women's Executive Network's ''Top 100 Most Powerful Women in Canada''.<ref name=":5" /><ref>{{Cite book|title=Who's who of Canadian women, 1999|date=1998|publisher=University of Toronto Press|others=Holmes, Gillian.|isbn=9781442683457|edition=9th|location=Toronto, Ont.|oclc=288093315}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.financialpost.com/magazine/Canadas+Most+Powerful+Women/3938673/story.html|title=Top 100 Canada's Most Powerful Women|first=Pamela|last=Jeffery|date=2010-12-06|access-date=2019-05-26|issn=1486-8008}}</ref> She has received honorary degrees from multiple universities, including the [[University of British Columbia]], the University of Edinburgh, [[MacEwan University]], and [[Memorial University of Newfoundland|Memorial University of Newfoundland and Labrador]].<ref name=":5" />

Armour has previously served as a chair for the Canadian Coalition of Women in Science, Engineering, Trades and Technology (CCWESTT).<ref name=":6" /> In 2010, Armour established the Canadian Centre for Women in Science, Engineering, Trades and Technology (WinSETT Centre), where she served as president of the board.<ref name=":5" /><ref name=":6" />

In September 2016, a 600-student large public school (K–9) in [[Ambleside, Edmonton|Ambleside]] (an [[Edmonton]] neighbourhood) was named after Armour (titled the Dr. Margaret-Ann Armour Edmonton Public School).<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://globalnews.ca/news/2068305/new-edmonton-school-to-be-named-after-former-councillor-michael-phair/|title=New Edmonton school to be named after former councillor Michael Phair – Edmonton {{!}} Globalnews.ca|date=2015-06-22|website=globalnews.ca|access-date=2019-05-26}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=https://edmontonjournal.com/news/local-news/edmonton-public-school-enrolment-tops-six-digits|title=Edmonton public school enrolment tops 100,000 students|website=Edmonton Journal|first=Janet|last=French |date=2018-10-15|access-date=2019-05-26}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://edmontonjournal.com/news/local-news/nuggets-busy-new-edmonton-catholic-school-has-rooms-that-move|title=St. John XXIII Catholic school set to open in Windermere|website=Edmonton Journal|first=Janet|last=French|date=2016-08-25|access-date=2019-05-26}}</ref><ref name=":7">{{Cite web|url=http://margaretannarmour.epsb.ca/aboutourschool/schoolprofile/|title=School Profile|website=margaretannarmour.epsb.ca|access-date=2019-05-26}}</ref> The school has since exceeded capacity.<ref name=":1" /> In addition, the University of Alberta's Working for Inclusivity in Chemistry group has launched a student-led speaker series in her name (Margaret-Ann Armour Lecture Series).<ref name=":5" />

Armour died, aged 79, on 25 May 2019.<ref name=":0" /> One day before her death, Armour received an honorary degree from the [[Concordia University of Edmonton]].<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":9" />
